case_study_insert.main_stem: Redcliff Spice Mills (RSM) is a sole trader in the food manufacturing industry, employing a workforce of 18. Founded in 2016 by Ezra Redcliff, the business supplies independent grocers with organic spices and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership rather than democratic leadership. RSM plans to invest $240,000 in a new automated spice-grinding and packing line, financed by a $180,000 bank loan, a $40,000 overdraft and $20,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $141,000 a year, a variable cost of $2.80 a unit and a selling price of $7.50, and produces 60,000 units a year. RSM faces two problems: labour turnover is high and spice waste has reached 5.4% of input.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Sales Report - Q3 2025: RSM milled 14,200 units of spice last quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 21 to 34 a month. Spice waste reached 5.4% of input. Delivery lead time averages 2.9 days. A survey of 320 buyers found 59% would pay up to $0.30 more for organic spices, and 43% check origin labels. A skills check shows 8 of 18 staff need training on the new grinding controls; local course fees are $560 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Redcliff Spice Mills as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.80%, increasing interest on RSM's $180,000 variable-rate loan and the $40,000 overdraft. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.50 to $13.19 an hour from April 2026. (3) Spice and pepper import prices have risen 14.2% year-on-year, food inflation is 7.1% and consumer spending on home-cooking spices grew 3.2%.

questions.question_text: RSM is financing a $240,000 expansion with a $180,000 bank loan, a $40,000 overdraft and $20,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for RSM of using the overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: An overdraft is flexible, letting Ezra Redcliff draw only the $40,000 needed when spice stock is bought and repay when grocers pay, so interest is charged on the actual shortfall. That suits a sole trader facing 5.4% spice waste and a 2.9-day delivery lead time, where cash needs change weekly, and it protects the $7.50 price from a permanently higher loan payment.

Point 2: An overdraft is quick to arrange and needs no long-term collateral, so RSM can act on the $240,000 grinding line without delaying for a new loan agreement. It complements the $180,000 loan by covering seasonal working capital while the $20,000 retained profit stays as a reserve. For a small workforce of 18, the simple arrangement saves management time, and it can be reduced as soon as the 59% of 320 buyers pay the $0.30 premium for organic spices. It also avoids a long-term interest commitment, so Ezra Redcliff is not locked into repayments if spice waste stays at 5.4%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: RSM is launching a new organic spice blend. Consider online marketplace advertising, trade fairs, or customer referral incentives. Which should RSM choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Online marketplace advertising: Listing ads on the marketplaces where independent grocers and home cooks already shop can target buyers of organic spices at low cost and be measured against the 14,200 units milled last quarter. It suits the 59% of 320 buyers who would pay $0.30 more and the 43% checking origin labels, with no stand fees. The limit is heavy competition online and the need for good product photos, which a workforce of 18 with high turnover may struggle to maintain.

Trade fairs: Fairs allow buyers to smell and taste blends and meet Ezra Redcliff, building trust in origin and quality, and can win several grocer contacts in one day. They are expensive once travel, stand and staff time are counted, and many visitors are not target customers; with a $180,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft, such spending is hard to justify for a sole trader.

Customer referral incentives: Offering a small discount to existing grocers who refer new ones costs little and uses trusted relationships, which suits a business with 2.9-day delivery and 5.4% waste. However, it grows slowly, rewards customers who would have bought anyway, and the discount cuts into the $4.70 contribution per unit needed to justify the $240,000 line.

Recommendation: RSM should choose online marketplace advertising. It reaches the 59% premium segment and the 43% checking labels at low, measurable cost and fits a small team. Trade fairs are rejected as too expensive given the $180,000 loan and overdraft; referrals are rejected because they are slow and discount the margin. RSM can add referral rewards later once the blend is established.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two options with advantages and disadvantages applied to RSM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of RSM with a justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

questions.question_text: RSM's labour turnover is high and spice waste has reached 5.4%. Explain two benefits for RSM of introducing a performance-related bonus for its milling staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bonus tied to output and waste gives the 18 staff a financial reason to reduce the 5.4% spice waste and the 2.6% defect rate, protecting the 14,200 units milled last quarter. Under autocratic leadership, where instructions are top-down, a bonus supplies extra motivation without Ezra Redcliff having to change his management style, improving the $7.50 product quality.

Point 2: Rewarding better performance can reduce the high labour turnover by making staff feel their effort is recognised, cutting the $560 per person training cost for the 8 of 18 still needing instruction on the new grinding controls. Because the bonus is paid only when results improve, it does not add a fixed cost to the $141,000 fixed costs, which matters while a $180,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft are being serviced and spice prices rise 14.2%. The bonus can be funded from the contribution saved when the 5.4% spice waste falls, so it partly pays for itself.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: RSM currently uses autocratic leadership. Consider keeping autocratic leadership or adopting democratic leadership for the new grinding line. Which should RSM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Autocratic leadership: Ezra Redcliff keeps full control of decisions, which suits a sole trader and can give quick, clear instructions on the new grinding controls, important when 8 of 18 staff still need training and spice waste is 5.4%. Decisions are fast and roles are unambiguous, helping protect the 14,200 units and the 2.9-day delivery lead time. The drawback is that high labour turnover suggests staff feel little ownership, and top-down orders may not surface practical ideas for cutting the 2.6% defect rate, while rigid control can worsen morale in a flat structure.

Democratic leadership: Consulting the 18 staff on grinding routines can generate ideas that reduce the 5.4% waste and the 2.6% defect rate, and involvement raises commitment, tackling labour turnover without paying every $560 course fee. It fits a flat structure and can help staff accept the $240,000 new line. The risks are slower decisions and disagreement under a sole trader who is used to control; with a $180,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft, delays could hurt output of 60,000 units.

Decision: RSM should adopt democratic leadership for the grinding line while keeping firm final authority. Consulting staff directly addresses the turnover and waste problems and uses their knowledge of the 14,200-unit process. Pure autocratic leadership is rejected because it has not stopped high turnover and suppresses the ideas needed to cut waste; full democracy is rejected because a $240,000 investment and tight cash need quick decisions, so a consultative approach with Ezra retaining the final say is the balanced choice.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two leadership styles with limited application to RSM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both styles in the context of RSM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both styles in the context of RSM with a well-justified decision covering speed, motivation and waste.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RSM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $141,000 / ($7.50 - $2.80) = $141,000 / $4.70 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $7.50 - $2.80 = $4.70. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.70.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RSM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with 60,000 units actual output, giving a margin of safety of 30,000 units, to judge whether the new grinding line should run at full capacity.
2. Use $4.70 contribution to test the $0.30 premium: if won, contribution becomes $5.00 ($4.70 + $0.30), showing how much volume could fall before profit disappears.
3. Combine $141,000 fixed costs with $4.70 contribution to set the volume needed to service the $180,000 loan and $40,000 overdraft before adding more capital.
4. Unit cost of $5.15 ($141,000 / 60,000 + $2.80) can be tracked to detect the 5.4% spice waste and 2.6% defect rate, protecting the $7.50 price.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.70 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 30,000-unit margin of safety; testing the $0.30 premium; loan and overdraft service targets; unit-cost benchmarking at $5.15.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RSM's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RSM's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.15 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.62 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.43 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $70,000 inventories + $58,000 trade receivables + $22,000 cash = $150,000; 2025 current assets = $84,000 + $50,000 + $14,000 = $148,000. Cover of the 2024 current liabilities of $130,000 was $150,000 / $130,000 = 1.15; cover of the 2025 liabilities of $148,000 was $148,000 / $148,000 = 1.00. Liquid assets excluding inventories were $150,000 - $70,000 = $80,000 in 2024, giving $80,000 / $130,000 = 0.62, and $148,000 - $84,000 = $64,000 in 2025, giving $64,000 / $148,000 = 0.43.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly weakened. Cover fell from 1.15 to 1.00, so in 2025 current assets only just equal current liabilities, leaving no cushion. The liquid-asset measure fell further, from 0.62 to 0.43, because cash dropped from $22,000 to $14,000 and inventories rose from $70,000 to $84,000 while receivables fell from $58,000 to $50,000. Although receivables were collected, the cash was not retained, and more value sits in slow-moving stock, risky when spice waste is 5.4%. With a $180,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft to service, RSM has little room for a late grocer payment.

Conclusion: RSM's liquidity has not improved. Both cover measures fell and the liquid-asset measure below 0.5 shows dependence on selling inventory. Ezra Redcliff should rebuild cash and slow the stock build before drawing more on the overdraft.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of the current-asset components and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RSM of sourcing certified organic spices for its blends.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certified organic spices support the 59% of 320 buyers who would pay $0.30 more and the 43% who check origin labels, so RSM can defend the $7.50 selling price and the $4.70 contribution per unit even as spice and pepper import prices rise 14.2%. Organic sourcing strengthens trust with independent grocers and fits the 14,200-unit blend launch, helping justify the $240,000 grinding line.

Disadvantage: Organic spice supplies usually cost more and can be less reliable, which would raise the $2.80 variable cost per unit or interrupt the 2.9-day delivery lead time. If a batch fails certification, the 2.6% defect rate and the 5.4% spice waste could worsen, adding cost to a sole trader already carrying a $180,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft. Rejected organic batches would also tie up the $20,000 retained profit in stock. Unless the full $0.30 premium is accepted, the higher input cost would squeeze contribution and threaten the 60,000-unit plan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.80%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in spice and pepper import prices will affect RSM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.80%): The increase is 0.80 percentage points. If RSM's $180,000 loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.80% x $180,000 = $1,440; a $40,000 overdraft would also cost more when used. That is noticeable against fixed costs of $141,000 but far below the $240,000 investment. Higher rates may slow grocer orders, yet the direct cost can be capped by fixing the loan or repaying the overdraft quickly.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.19): RSM employs 18 staff, but the insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. Productivity is 60,000 units / 18 staff = about 3,333 units per worker. If that holds, the rise can be absorbed within the $2.80 variable cost and $4.70 contribution; if high labour turnover lowers output, unit labour cost rises. It is a permanent rise but cannot be quantified from the insert.

Input price inflation (14.2% spice and pepper): The insert does not decompose the $2.80 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is valid: if all of the $2.80 rose 14.2%, that is 14.2% x $2.80 = about $0.40 per unit, or roughly $24,000 a year at 60,000 units. That directly erodes the $4.70 contribution servicing the $180,000 loan and $40,000 overdraft. RSM can recover part through the $0.30 premium accepted by 59% of buyers.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in spice and pepper import prices will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit and repeatedly cuts the $4.70 margin that funds the new line, far outweighing the $1,440 interest effect; the wage rise matters but is unquantifiable and partly offset by strong productivity, whereas imported input inflation attacks the margin directly.
